name: מְפִיבֹשֶׁת
gloss: from the mouth of shame (“shame” for Baal); first part uncertain
summary: Two men of Saul's house. Jonathan's son, lame in both feet from the day the news of Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel and his nurse fled (2Sa 4:4); David showed him kindness for Jonathan's sake and he ate at the king's table (2Sa 9:6–13); Ziba slandered him when David fled from Absalom, and he came to meet the king unwashed and in mourning (2Sa 16:1–4; 19:25–31); David spared him for the oath of Yahweh between him and Jonathan (2Sa 21:7). Chronicles calls him מְרִיב בַּעַל (1Ch 8:34; 9:40). The other is Saul's son by Rizpah, handed to the Gibeonites (2Sa 21:8–9). The second part is the noun בֹּשֶׁת “shame”, which the prophets use for Baal (Jer 11:13; Hos 9:10) and which stands in Samuel where Chronicles has בַּעַל, as in Ish-bosheth for Eshbaal; the first part מְפִי is read as “from the mouth of”, but scripture does not explain it.

evidence.note: Jonathan's son, lame in his feet, “and his name was מְפִיבֹשֶׁת”.
“Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul came to David and fell on his face.”
“Mephibosheth (וּמְפִבֹשֶׁת) the son of Saul came down to meet the king; he had not dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes.”
“The king spared מְפִי־בֹשֶׁת son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of the oath of Yahweh.”
“The son of Jonathan was מְרִיב בַּעַל”: the same man, with בַּעַל where Samuel has בֹּשֶׁת.
Saul's son by Rizpah, “Armoni and Mephibosheth (מְפִבֹשֶׁת)”.
“Altars to the shame (לַבֹּשֶׁת), altars to burn incense to Baal”: בֹּשֶׁת as a name for Baal.

note: Takes m.da.ay (the name in all its spellings: מְפִיבֹשֶׁת, מְפִבֹשֶׁת, and מְפִי בֹשֶׁת written as two words at 2Sa 21:7). The surface בֹשֶׁת of that verse is also filed under b.ax.ad by spelling. names/merib-baal (under baal) already tags Mephibosheth@2Sa.4.4 for the Chronicles form; this entry tags him too, as eshbaal and ish-bosheth both tag Saul's son. The first element מְפִי is uncertain: “from the mouth of” (מִן + פֶּה) is one reading; others take it from a verb (נפה, פאה “scatter, blow away”, giving “scatterer of shame”). The gloss gives the first as one reading only; no verse decides it, and a reviewer may prefer to gloss only the second element.
